title: Chinese official says economy resilient but recovery momentum remains weak
full_text:
BEIJING, Oct 20 (Reuters) - China’s economy has withstood pressure and continues to expand steadily, but the recovery foundation and momentum are relatively weak, an economic official at the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) told a press conference on Tuesday.
The comments were made following the release of better-than-expected economic growth data for the third quarter on Monday, as roaring exports offset consumers’ tight grip on their wallets.
• The impact of external shocks is deepening, while a mismatch between strong supply and weak demand at home remains pronounced, said Zuo Gang, deputy director for the Department of National Economic Comprehensive Affairs at the NDRC, which is the country’s top economic planner.
• Divergence across industries is also evident, and the foundation and the momentum for a sustained economic recovery remain weak, he added.
• The NDRC is drafting an implementation plan for the strategy to expand domestic demand for 2026-2030 and will accelerate efforts to issue and implement it, Zuo said.

title: US to launch $8 billion support program for farmers to offset diesel costs, Trump says
full_text:
S&P rises and Nasdaq jumps over 1%, rebounding after their worst week since June
By Bo Erickson and Kanishka Singh
PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the US Department of Agriculture will launch what he called a new "harvest fuel relief program" that will provide farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.
"Tonight, I’m also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new harvest fuel relief program, providing our farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season," Trump said in a midterm election campaign speech in Kansas.
The announcement was the latest in a series of financial promises and pledges that the Republican leader has made to voters heading into the November midterm elections, where control of Congress is at stake.
The Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. However, Trump’s approval rating has been low due to his handling of the high cost of living for Americans during the US-Israeli war on Iran that has raised fuel prices.
Trump and the Republican Party have been scrambling to maintain support in farm states with competitive Senate races as costs have risen.
Trump signed an executive order earlier this month that he said would expand access to tax-exempt diesel.
The Department of Agriculture said after Trump’s speech on Monday that it would make $8 billion available "for one-time payments to American farmers this harvest season to provide relief during temporary market disruptions and increased input costs."
The program will provide what the department called "proportional support to producers using a uniform formula to cover a portion of modeled losses during the 2026 crop year."
The $8 billion in payments would be administered by the department’s Farm Service Agency, the department said.
Trump has also separately proposed sending $5,000 checks to all adult citizens if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate in the midterms, though analysts, economists and even some Republicans in Congress have reacted with skepticism.
Earlier this month, Trump said the US government would send a one-time payment of $90 to more than 20 million Americans enrolled in Medicare, a health insurance program for the elderly.

title: Micron union in Taiwan to launch strike as bonus dispute escalates
full_text:

By Wen-Yee Lee
TAIPEI, Oct 20 (Reuters) - A union representing Micron Technology workers in Taoyuan, Taiwan, said it would launch a strike on Thursday to coincide with a mediation meeting between the US chipmaker and another collective representing workers at its Taichung operations, escalating a dispute over employee bonuses.
The strike raises the stakes in a labour dispute at one of Micron’s most important manufacturing hubs, where it produces DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, key components in AI servers.
The Taoyuan union said the strike was intended to show solidarity with the Taichung union and to increase pressure on Micron to put forward a concrete profit-sharing proposal.
Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan, with separate unions representing workers at its Taoyuan and Taichung operations. The company has said it has invested more than T$1.6 trillion ($49 billion) on the island.
Mediation between Micron and the Taoyuan union ended without an agreement in September. The union secured authorisation from its members to strike in early October.
The Taichung union, which represents workers at Micron’s largest operation in Taiwan, remains in negotiations with the company. It has yet to hold a vote on whether to strike.
The Taoyuan union did not specify how long the solidarity strike would last, saying it would release further details on Thursday.
"Through our actions, we will make our dissatisfaction with the current system heard and demonstrate our determination to establish a fair profit-sharing system," the Taoyuan union said in a statement on Monday.
Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te called last week for Micron and its workers to negotiate "sincerely".

title: Exclusive-India probing Pernod, Diageo Scotch imports under India-UK trade pact, sources say
full_text:
S&P rises and Nasdaq jumps over 1%, rebounding after their worst week since June
By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Indian tax officials are investigating whether liquor giants Pernod Ricard and Diageo wrongly classified some bulk Scotch imports, allowing them to pay lower tariffs introduced under the recently agreed India-UK trade pact, five industry sources familiar with the matter said.
Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India and embroiled companies like Samsung, LG and Volkswagen. They often involve large back-tax demands raised years after the items were imported, with Indian officials saying they are only enforcing the law.
Last week, tax inspectors made an unexpected visit to Pernod’s India headquarters near New Delhi where they questioned company executives about their Scotch imports, three of the people said.
Diageo’s Indian unit, United Spirits, in a stock exchange filing last week said its offices in multiple locations were searched on Friday as part of an "industry-wide exercise" by authorities, without saying what the search related to. The other two people said Diageo is also being investigated for how it classifies some Scotch imports.
Pernod told Reuters in a statement that it is cooperating with the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and providing all information requested, adding it was committed to addressing any questions from the authorities. Diageo, also in a statement, said it is cooperating with Indian authorities, and has always complied with local laws. In its stock exchange disclosure, it said it had provided all documents and clarifications.
The Indian revenue directorate did not respond to a request for comment.
Reuters is first to report that tax inspectors visited Pernod’s India office, and publish details of the probe, including that it is linked to the UK-India tariff declarations.
BULK SCOTCH IMPORTS
Diageo and France’s Pernod Ricard dominate India’s $65 billion alcohol market. Both companies import bulk Scotch concentrates in containers to mix with other ingredients to make brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s.
Under the trade pact, which took effect on July 15, India agreed to slash import taxes on certain Scotch imports to 75%, from 150%.
The tax inspectors argued that the duty relief did not apply to bulk concentrates, four of the people said.
"The tax department is concerned that bulk imports are being wrongly classified," one of them said.
ICONIC PRODUCT
The UK accounts for almost 75% of India’s imported spirits market, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, Crisil Ratings said this year.
In July, the British government said "iconic UK products" including whiskies and gin would benefit from India’s tariff changes. It added that the UK’s whisky exports to the country were worth more than £200 million in 2022.
Pernod is already facing antitrust cases in India, its biggest market by volume, and a $314 million back-tax demand for allegedly undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing.
Diageo in August agreed to reformulate some of its most popular drinks after the country’s food safety regulator banned them in some states for adding flavours against regulations.
During the visit to Pernod’s India office on Thursday, tax inspectors reviewed some documents related to bulk Scotch imports, but have not been in contact since, said one of the people.

Netflix and United Airlines are among the highlights of the quarterly earnings agenda, OpenAI is reportedly racing to raise $30 billion ahead of Anthropic's much-anticipated initial public offering.
1. Futures mixed
U.S. stock futures were mixed on Tuesday. By 03:17 ET (07:17 GMT), the Dow futures contract had risen by 163 points, or 0.3%, S&P 500 futures had ticked up by 7 points, or 0.1%, and Nasdaq 100 futures had fallen by 62 points, or 0.2%.
The main averages on Wall Street finished around both sides of the flatline in the prior session. The benchmark S&P 500 gained 0.41% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.11%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average edged down by 0.07%.
Tech stocks were among the standout performers, with the Nasdaq notching its best day in two weeks and a tracker of the chip industry breaking an eight-session run of declines. Given the concentration of tech in the broader index, this helped lift the S&P despite a pullback in almost two-thirds of components within the average, analysts at Deutsche Bank said.
AI names, in particular, stabilized after a selloff driven by concerns over debt-driven spending and elevated borrowing costs. However, the AI trade reversed course once again this morning, dragging down the KOSPI in South Korea and the Nikkei in Japan.
2. Oil prices climb
Elsewhere, oil prices jumped, leaving benchmark Brent crude futures last exchanging hands above $110 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures have also increased by around 1% to $99.53 a barrel.
Brent settled within touching distance of a five-month high on Monday, even though it had fallen earlier in the session on reports that the U.S. and Iran may have reached a breakthrough in mediated negotiations.
However, that decline had a short shelf life. Oil prices surged once again after Iran's First Vice President said the country had "no choice but to exercise sovereignty" over the Strait of Hormuz, exacerbating worries over crude supply disruptions in the critical chokepoint.
Recent strikes on vessels near Hormuz have slowed the flow of oil through the waterway. Hormuz has been largely shuttered since after the start of a joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran in late February, although reported shipping figures have indicated that supplies showed signs of recovery last month.
3. Netflix to report
Meanwhile, Netflix is due to report after the close on Tuesday.
Last week, the streaming titan reportedly said it planned to slash around 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 roles. The jobs impacted would mostly be in the firm’s product, legal, tech and human-resources units, the Wall Street Journal reported.
It was the biggest round of job reductions at the company since 2022. At the end of last year, Netflix employed about 16,000 workers.
The move comes as Netflix is grappling with easing customer engagement after years of strong growth that put intense pressure on traditional cable television businesses. A failed bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery’s streaming and studio assets earlier this year has also exacerbated concerns around the group’s overall strategy.
4. United Airlines earnings ahead
United Airlines is also scheduled to report after the close of U.S. markets.

title: Europe’s earnings boom widens beyond energy and AI
full_text:

By Samuel Indyk
LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - European companies are expected to deliver another quarter of exceptional earnings growth, again driven mainly by profits at energy companies and those pivotal to the datacentre buildout, although signs are emerging of strength elsewhere.
Third-quarter earnings for the pan-regional STOXX 600 are expected to grow 20.7% from a year ago, according to LSEG I/B/E/S, a slowdown from the second-quarter pace of 24%, but still among the fastest in years.
With over half of the index’s market capitalisation reporting over the next two weeks, here is what you need to know as the earnings season begins:
1/ WHERE ARE THE DOWNGRADES?
In the past, analysts have typically cut earnings estimates ahead of reporting season. This time, in aggregate, they have raised forecasts, suggesting better-than-expected growth, optimism over AI spending and elevated energy prices will lead to stronger profit growth.
"Some of these dynamics look a little different than usual," David Groman, global equity strategist at Citi, said, adding they were "unseasonably strong and unusually broad".
Pre-earnings upgrades could make investors focus less on whether companies beat their third-quarter estimates and more on their outlook for the fourth quarter and beyond for clues on whether momentum can continue.
2/ ALL ABOUT AI
Europe lacks AI big-hitters, such as Nvidia, Alphabet or Samsung Electronics, but it has many smaller hardware stocks, materials and industrials that are benefiting from the capex boom.
Tech earnings are forecast to increase by almost 33% from a year ago, according to LSEG I/B/E/S, while industrials profits are expected to rise by 11%.
"It’s often said Europe doesn’t really have any AI plays but we think you can pick through French and German industrials," said Dorian Carrell, head of multi-asset income at Schroders.
"Expectations there have been tempered over the last few weeks, but there is a chance for European industrials to surpass expectations."
3/ ENERGY BOOST
The rise in oil and gas prices internationally since the outbreak of the US-Iran war has increased inflation and is a cost for many, but it has also boosted earnings expectations for companies that can benefit.
"The big reason for the continued upgrades for earnings this year in Europe has been the tailwind from energy prices," Barclays equity strategists said.
That support could fade if tensions in the Middle East ease and energy prices retreat, or if sustained high prices curb demand, turning the energy sector from a boost to a drag on broader earnings growth.
"We expect refining-geared names to outperform, and we think the question now is: how long this lasts," Barclays added.
4/ BANKING BOUNCE?
Europe’s banks, one of the best-performing sectors in global equities over the last four years, have come under pressure from political concerns, but analysts do not anticipate a poor earnings season.
Europe’s bank index is down 7% since the start of September, compared to a 1.7% drop for the broader STOXX 600, offering a lower bar to clear.
The sector trades at about 10 times its forward earnings, which are expected to grow at about 8% over the medium term, a backdrop that should support the sector going forward, according to Schroders’ Carrell, especially as recent volatility has depressed expectations.
"The capital positions are strong, but the key thing is the lending activity picking up," Carrell said.
"Everything points to European banks being in a good place."
5/ CONSUMER RESILIENCE
Worries about consumers lacking spending power have lingered in Europe for years, but Maximilian Uleer, head of European equity and cross-asset strategy at Deutsche Bank, is upbeat.
Trading at 13.6 times forward earnings, Europe’s consumer staples sector trades at a 35% discount to its US counterpart, which Uleer thinks is too low.
"I prefer European staples over US staples, because of the valuation difference and similar earnings profile," Uleer said. The European staples sector is expected to grow earnings by over 7% in the third quarter.
"There’s good reason to believe that the consumer is more resilient than we think, especially in Europe, and that’s why we like staples. I think people will be surprised by more positive numbers."

title: As France erupts, Europe’s far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections
full_text:
S&P rises and Nasdaq jumps over 1%, rebounding after their worst week since June
By Michel Rose, Angelo Amante and Miranda Murray
PARIS/ROME/BERLIN, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island’s role as a breadbasket since Roman times.
But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting.
As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland.
Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany’s former Communist east looking for alternatives.
The US-Iran war, which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending.
The discontent has spilled onto the streets.
In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris’ northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country’s worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire.
"Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying," said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes.
"Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. It’s terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become."
The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly €100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140% and diesel prices have doubled.
In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the "legitimate demands" of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. "We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted," he said.
PROTESTS ERUPT ACROSS EUROPE
Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and looting stores during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs.
In Gela, on Sicily’s southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. "We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," said one banner.
"We are completely at a standstill," said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers’ representative in Caltanissetta province. "The (fuel) cost has more than doubled."
Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies.
Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal’s centre-right government.
In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home sparked nationwide demonstrations over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month.
Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while large rallies in Albania have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent.
Concerns about purchasing power have become "a major driver of populist politics" across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po.
Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe’s mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine.
LE PEN MAKES FUEL PRICES A CAMPAIGN ISSUE
The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April’s presidential election. Macron’s government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets.
Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns.
“Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen,” said Ivaldi. “I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time."
Since the Iran war began, Le Pen’s ratings have improved while Macron’s have slipped, according to polling by Elabe.
Le Pen’s proposal to sharply cut value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential.
CALLS TO RESTORE RUSSIA TIES
In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after strong gains in local elections. The cost of living topped Germans’ concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month.
German inflation spiked to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9%, handing ammunition to the AfD to attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, arguing that Berlin’s support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europe’s largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling.
Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich.
“Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices ... rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them," he said.
“These geopolitical shocks are ... much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle."
The argument is gaining traction elsewhere.
In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci that advocates restoring gas links with Russia.
In Poland, one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany.
“I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning,” he said.

title: When do chip stocks tend to peak? Analyst examines historical returns
full_text:
Investing.com -- Truist said in a note Tuesday that peak fundamentals and peak stock returns for semiconductors are still ahead, noting that chip stocks have historically peaked about one quarter after fundamentals.
“Semi fundamentals are in a SuperCycle condition - posting much faster growth for a much longer duration than even the Tech Bubble of 1998-2001,” analyst William Stein wrote.
Consensus is said to suggest fourth-quarter 2026 revenue growth of 74% year over year. That quarter would mark the 15th consecutive quarter of improvement and could be the peak, according to Stein.
He added that by comparison, demand usually peaks at 29% growth in the seventh quarter. The tech bubble peaked at 50% growth, and that cycle had already crashed by the 14th quarter.
Stein attributed the cycle’s strength mainly to data center and AI demand. He added that the cycle’s out-of-phase nature, with industrial demand recovering later, is extending its duration.
Contrary to conventional wisdom that stocks lead fundamentals by two quarters, Truist found that semi stocks have on average peaked one quarter after revenue growth.
“This implies semi stocks should continue to deliver positive returns at least through 1Q27, but potentially much longer, depending on whether fundamental growth upticks in the next few quarters, which would not surprise us,” Stein commented.
The analyst also pointed to the SOX’s 29% pullback from June 22 to July 29. He noted that drops of this size that did not lead to downturns are rare.
“To us, this means that, assuming fundamentals remain sound, further downside is limited,” Stein wrote. “We view upcoming earnings as a likely stabilization catalyst for most of our coverage.”

However, it favors Buy-rated companies with “fragile” business models, including Vishay, Arrow Electronics, Avnet, Diodes and Sensata.

OSLO/KYIV, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy was due on Tuesday in Oslo to meet US special envoy Steve Witkoff, trying to repair ties that have deteriorated this month as President Donald Trump courted Moscow.
Trump, who has waived sanctions on Russia in what he says is an effort to lower US fuel prices, has repeatedly rebuked Zelenskiy and called for him to be replaced.
Kyiv says Washington has lately failed to provide early warning of Russian missile launches, throttled SpaceX’s Starshield satellite links that guide Ukrainian drones, and failed to deliver air defences paid for by European allies.
In the latest comments expressing warmth towards Moscow and coldness towards Kyiv, Trump said on Monday: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine." Zelenskiy was "not helping matters much" and Kyiv should find "somebody else to negotiate".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged on Tuesday that a consignment of US air defence missiles bought by Europeans for Ukraine may not have been delivered, but played down the significance.
"I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he told journalists during a visit to India.
The Kremlin said it was hoping to set up a meeting soon between Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, an apparent indication that Witkoff could head to Russia after meeting Zelenskiy.
RUSSIA STEPS UP ATTACKS
As US ties with Ukraine have deteriorated, Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukrainian cities, particularly targeting power stations and fuel in apparent defiance of a call from Trump for both sides to spare each other’s energy systems.
Ukraine held back for several days from hitting Russian oil refineries in deference to Trump’s request but resumed strikes after no sign Russia was complying. Both sides have also struck data centres.
Trump has criticised the Ukrainian attacks on Russia while saying little about Russia’s more severe attacks on Ukraine, which Kyiv says have become even more intense and deadlier because of the withdrawal of US technology to fend them off.
In the latest attacks, Ukrainian officials said a Russian drone struck near a petrol station on a highway heading south out of Kyiv, killing three people and setting cars ablaze.
Footage released by Ukraine’s emergency services of a separate attack on a warehouse in the capital that also killed three people showed firefighters battling a huge blaze, surrounded by twisted wreckage.
Energy facilities were attacked in seven Ukrainian regions overnight, knocking out power, and the western Lviv region was struck again during the day. Three other people were reported killed in Kramatorsk in the east.
ZELENSKIY SPEAKS TO RUBIO
Zelenskiy said he had spoken with Rubio about ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian attacks and "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored".
"Of course, all of this comes against the backdrop of our diplomatic efforts to end this horrific war and the constant killing of people," Zelenskiy said in a post on X.
The deterioration of relations began 10 days ago when Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal agreed with Putin, which he said would help reduce prices. High fuel costs since Trump launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans before legislative elections next month.
Trump has since repeatedly berated Zelenskiy over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are one of its few ways of fighting back after nearly five years of intensive Russian bombardment.
Trump later issued a broad waiver for tougher sanctions on Russia that were meant to have begun this week.
Washington denies withholding intelligence from Kyiv or imposing curbs on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink communications system.
Kyiv says the satellite receptors no longer work when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones. SpaceX boss Elon Musk has said Starshield is controlled by the US government and any limits on its use are ultimately up to Trump.
Western European countries consider defending Ukraine from Russia’s invasion to be an existential issue for European security and have strongly backed Zelenskiy, seeking to head off a deeper rupture between Washington and Kyiv.
The United States under Trump has largely stopped providing weapons to Ukraine but lets European countries buy them on Kyiv’s behalf. It also provides intelligence and technology that Europe cannot match.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the goal of hosting Tuesday’s Oslo meetings was "to steer the diplomatic efforts onto a more constructive path".
Finland is co-hosting the talks. Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he would attend to discuss "Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and the overall security situation in Europe."
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who has led US negotiating efforts with Witkoff, was expected to attend meetings virtually, Norway said. Zelenskiy, Stubb and Stoere will hold a press conference on Tuesday.

title: Federal Reserve seen skipping Oct rate hike but hiking in Dec - Reuters poll
full_text:
Investing.com - The Federal Reserve is set to keep interest rates steady at the central bank's next monetary policy meeting later this month, but raise borrowing costs once again in December, according to a Reuters poll released on Tuesday.
Some 94 out of 100 economists who responded to the poll taken between October 16-20 said they expect rates to remain at a range of 3.75% to 4.00% following the October 27-28 gathering.
Meanwhile, all 100 anticipate that the Fed will increase rates at its final meeting of the year on December 8-9, Reuters said. That is up sharply from the prior poll, in which less than half of the economists predicted a December hike.
Last month, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee lifted borrowing costs for the first time since 2023, citing a desire to corral mounting inflationary pressures fueled by soaring energy prices.
But investors are widely wagering that the Fed will opt to skip another hike this month, even though recent price growth data for September came in hotter than anticipated.
Instead, traders have been keeping tabs on messaging from Fed officials. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, sticking to a strategy he has adopted since taking over at the helm of the central bank earlier this year, has declined to provide any specific guidance.
Others, including San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, have argued that while more rate increases may be needed in the future, there is currently no urgent need to hike immediately. New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson have also expressed a preference to evaluate more economic data before pulling the trigger on a fresh rate bump.
Almost 60% of the economists polled by Reuters expect the policy rate to reach a peak of 4.00% to 4.25%, although some flagged risks that the Fed may opt to roll out more rate increases than initially thought.

title: Anthropic revenue hits $16.3 billion as preliminary S-1 outlines IPO risks - WSJ
full_text:
U.S. stocks rise as tech fluctuations offset by earnings moves, fall in oil prices
Investing.com -- Artificial intelligence leader Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANTP) is laying the groundwork for a mega-initial public offering that could value the company at $2 trillion, revealing exponential top-line expansion alongside staggering long-term capital commitments. According to a draft prospectus viewed by The Wall Street Journal, the San Francisco-based firm generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, marking a dramatic surge from $1.1 billion in the same period last year.
Behind the breakneck operational expansion lies an increasingly capital-intensive model driven by the relentless demand for processing power. Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first six months of 2026 alone, surpassing its total infrastructure expenditure of $7.3 billion for the entirety of 2025, according to the Journal.
To secure necessary capacity, the company has locked in massive, noncancelable obligations that highlight both its operational scale and structural vulnerabilities. The report indicates that Anthropic is committed to roughly $450 billion in cloud compute agreements over the next decade, including $111 billion with Google Cloud, $110 billion with Amazon Web Services, and $31 billion with Microsoft.
Anthropic indicated it could potentially spend $750 billion in the coming years on obtaining more computing capacity, including deals it is still actively negotiating.
The sheer volume of these commitments underscores a growing tension between Anthropic and its primary infrastructure partners. The company reportedly acknowledged in its filing that it has sought more capacity than hyperscalers were willing to supply, prompting Anthropic to pursue third-party data center developments to bypass compute bottlenecks.
Despite surging top-line growth, financial disclosures reveal complex balance sheet dynamics and concentrated counterparty exposure. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of 2026, though $72 billion of that total stemmed from non-cash accounting adjustments related to convertible notes and financing instruments.
Concentration risk remains a key consideration for prospective investors as the company prepares its public debut. The Journal observed that approximately 20% of Anthropic’s $16.3 billion first-half revenue was derived from just two customers, with the firm anticipating that a limited client base will continue to generate a significant portion of total revenue for the foreseeable future.
Beyond financial metrics, the preliminary S-1 filing devotes substantial attention to operational risks and catastrophic liability management. According to the report, the company highlighted potential risks surrounding model alignment and catastrophic incidents, explicitly noting that potential damages from severe AI-related security events could exceed available insurance coverage limits.
Governance disclosures further detail the executive compensation structure and ownership commitments of co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei. The Chief Executive and President each drew base salaries of roughly $655,000 in 2025, according to the report, while both leaders pledged 80% of their personal equity to philanthropic endeavors alongside the creation of a 5% public benefit fund.

title: SpaceX and Tesla form special committees to evaluate potential merger, Musk says
full_text:
Investing.com -- SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA) have each established independent special committees to explore a potential merger, Chief Executive Elon Musk confirmed during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call. The disclosure formalizes years of market speculation that Musk would consolidate his corporate empire, a trajectory that accelerated following SpaceX's acquisition of xAI in February and its subsequent June public offering.
Musk emphasized that while independent directors are actively evaluating the transaction, negotiations remain in early stages with no guarantee of an agreement. Speaking to investors, Musk acknowledged his role as a conflicted party, describing the process as "this sort of odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can't be in the conversation."
The strategic logic behind a prospective combination centers heavily on advancing artificial intelligence and hardware capabilities across both platforms. Musk highlighted significant potential synergies in "developing super intelligence software, chip design, Terafab, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, and connectivity," suggesting the two companies are already converging as the industry approaches a broader technological inflection point.
Despite the strategic merits, securing investor approval presents a substantial structural hurdle for the proposed deal. Any transaction will require the support of 50% of all outstanding Tesla shares, a threshold Musk explicitly characterized as "quite a high hurdle to achieve."
Wall Street analysts and institutional investors have increasingly viewed a combination as an inevitable step toward streamlining Musk’s broader ambitions. Barclays analyst Dan Levy recently posited that SpaceX could act as the primary acquirer in an all-stock transaction, a structure that would allow Musk to consolidate voting control over critical AI initiatives including Tesla's Optimus humanoid robot and SpaceX's Grok chatbot.
Market reaction following the revelation reflects heightened expectations that the long-discussed consolidation may finally materialize. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, underscored the shifting landscape following the call, noting on social media that the "odds of SPCX and TSLA combo just inched up" while estimating a "95% chance in the next two years."
The merger discussions come against the backdrop of blowout financial results for SpaceX, which delivered $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, comfortably ahead of Wall Street consensus estimates of $12.87 billion. The company’s top-line growth accelerated 161% year-over-year, while net income reached $4.4 billion, further reinforcing SpaceX's financial position as it considers expanding its capital footprint.

title: Netflix shares fall over 5% after hours on soft current quarter revenue guidance
full_text:
Wall Street ends higher on surge in health care stocks, solid earnings
Investing.com -- Netflix on Tuesday delivered a quarterly bottom-line beat, but its current quarter revenue guidance missed consensus estimates, sending shares of the company down more than 5% after hours.
The streaming pioneer’s results come at a time when it has been struggling with user engagement and continued capital spending to sustain its vast portfolio of content. Shares of Netflix have fallen 0.4% since the company’s last quarterly report in July, and have lost 26.7% YTD versus a 12.7% rise in the broader S&P 500.
The quarterly report also comes at a time when Netflix has seen two high-profile executive departures in the span of a week, with chief content officer Bela Bajaria being replaced by former Fox and Disney media executive Peter Rice, and film division head Dan Lin leaving after nearly three years at the helm.
NFLX last week said it would eliminate about 1,000 jobs, or 6% of its global workforce, in the biggest round of layoffs since 2022.
To keep viewership elevated, Netflix has been broadening its programming mix beyond on-demand films and television, adding live events, sports, video podcasts and content from YouTube creators. It has also pursued programming channels and bundling arrangements with other streaming services as it looks to increase the time users spend on its platform.
The company has secured the rights to broadcast the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra. Earlier this month, NFLX also secured the license of a slate of movies and television shows from Disney, including titles such as Ice Age and Percy Jackson.
Netflix in July had also said it would reduce the frequency of its viewing-hours report, publishing the data annually instead of twice a year starting in January 2027, in a move to shift investor focus toward its core financial metrics, including revenue and operating profit. The firm stopped reporting quarterly subscriber numbers in 2025.
Goldman Sachs recently said third-party data on Netflix’s engagement metrics had been “quite mixed” this summer into fall. Citing Sensor Tower data, the brokerage had highlighted a 10% Y/Y decline in U.S. monthly active users in Q3, compared to a 1% decline in the rest of the world.
"We’ll continue to expand our entertainment offering through licensing and new ways to bringnmore third-party content to our service, like our TF1 partnership in France. Our audience, which is approaching one billion people, and our best-in-class product capabilities, make us great partners for studios, networks and creative talent," NFLX said in a letter to shareholders.
"Member response to our 2026 price changes is consistent with prior adjustments and our expectations, an indicator that our engagement - which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing - remains healthy and that we continue to deliver strong value to members," Netflix added.
The streaming firm earned 87 cents per share on revenue of $12.87 billion for Q3 2026. Analysts had expected a profit of 82 cents per share on revenue of $12.87 billion.
For Q4, Netflix expects revenue of $13.4 billion. Analysts had anticipated revenue of $13.51 billion.
For the full-year 2026, NFLX now sees revenue of $51.1 billion, compared to $51 billion to $51.4 billion previously. Netflix said the new annual guidance was "0.2% below the mid-point" of the prior range.
"While subscription revenue growth has outperformed our expectations, we currently expect 2026 ad revenue of ~$2.7B vs. approximately $3B previously (due to slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities)," the company added.

title: Apple’s $1,999 foldable phone is set to hit stores Friday, are you buying one?
full_text:
Investing.com -- Apple's (NASDAQ:AAPL) first foldable iPhone hits retail stores this Friday, October 23, with a starting price of $1,999 for the 256GB model. But buyers hoping to get their hands on the device anytime soon may face a long wait. Apple described pre-orders for the Duo as “nothing short of extraordinary,” with online delivery estimates slipping to late January 2027 within hours of pre-orders opening on Friday, October 16. The company has also reportedly advised retail staff to caution customers against expecting to buy the device in-store without a pre-order, according to MacRumors.
For investors, the early rush raises a key question: will strong launch demand translate into a sustained earnings boost, or is it largely a product of limited supply? Priced 82% above the iPhone Pro, the foldable faces a dual challenge: sustaining demand at a premium price point while meeting orders amid ongoing memory shortages. Apple reports fourth-quarter results on November 2nd.
What Apple is selling — and at what price
The Duo is a book-style foldable featuring a 5.4-inch external display and a 7.6-inch internal screen, powered by the A20 Pro chip and a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system running iOS 27. The titanium-framed device starts at $1,999 for 256GB and scales to $3,199 at the 2TB tier, a configuration that sits above every previous iPhone Pro Max in Apple's pricing history. That 2TB price point is not just a premium option, it is a new ceiling that redefines what the market will pay for an Apple handset.
Foldables represent just over 2% of global smartphone units but roughly 7% of total industry revenue, per IDC background data, meaning Apple is entering a niche that already punches well above its unit weight in dollar terms. If the Duo captures even a modest slice of Apple's roughly 1.4 billion active iPhone users, the ASP uplift is material.
Bull case: ASP reset and a new upgrade cycle
The bull thesis rests on average selling price, not just unit volume. Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that if Pro owners trade up to the base Duo, Apple's iPhone ASP could rise 82%; the uplift from Pro Max owners would be 67%. Those figures frame the Duo less as a standalone product and more as a lever on the entire iPhone revenue line.
Bloomberg Intelligence analysts said Duo sales could exceed their prior estimate of 14 million units and $28 billion in revenue for Apple's fiscal 2027, though the analysts themselves described that revision as preliminary given the supply uncertainty still in play. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives projects around 10 million units over the coming quarters and up to 25 million in 2027, calling early demand "well ahead of supply out of the gates." JPMorgan, which reiterated its Overweight rating on Apple on Monday, October 19, noted that delivery timelines extending beyond three months reflect both genuine demand strength and an already well-understood supply ramp challenge.
If in-store walk-in inventory on Friday, October 23 clears within the first hour and delivery windows remain in late January, that would confirm the demand-over-supply dynamic is durable rather than a pre-order spike.
Bear case: scarcity theater and shipment cuts
The bear counterpoint is real, and it comes from inside the analyst community rather than from gadget skeptics. Loop Capital downgraded Apple on Tuesday and says it sees no recovery in cut iPhone shipments, adding a note of structural caution to the launch-week euphoria. Analyst Ananda Baruah said Apple’s previously reduced iPhone shipments may no longer be recoverable by 2027, despite the cuts being driven by memory and processor supply constraints rather than weak demand. The analyst also sees lower ASPs next year, suggesting the Duo will provide no boost.
Counterpoint Research's estimate of roughly 6 million Duo units for 2026 sits at less than half of the Yorkville Ives projection for the same period. That gap, 6 million versus 10 million, with a longer-range spread reaching 25 million, is unusually wide even by foldable-category standards, and it reflects a genuine analytical disagreement: is the sell-out a demand signal or a supply-rationing artifact? Apple has not disclosed how many units were built for launch or how many pre-orders it received, making it impossible to separate the two explanations with available public data.
The Street consensus, per JPMorgan, has actually trimmed 2026 calendar-year Duo volume projections from 10 million to 8 to 9 million units, acknowledging that supply will gate near-term numbers regardless of demand. For the stock, that revision matters less than the fiscal 2027 trajectory, which remains the real earnings test.
Base case: a meaningful but back-half story
The most defensible read is that the Duo is a genuine product cycle event for Apple, but one whose financial impact will be back-loaded into fiscal 2027 rather than front-loaded into the current quarter. The supply ramp constraints are acknowledged by JPMorgan and implicit in delivery windows that stretch into late January 2027. That timing means Q4 FY2026 earnings on November 2 will offer limited Duo revenue, the device launches three days before that quarter ends in a calendar sense, and management's color on the supply ramp and FY2027 guidance will matter more than any single-quarter Duo shipment figure.
Apple also announced today new and expanded partnerships with American titanium and camera technology suppliers for the Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, suggesting the company is actively working to broaden its component base. That move could incrementally ease the supply constraint heading into the holiday quarter, though the timeline for additional capacity coming online is not yet public.
What to monitor heading into November 2
The immediate data points arrive in sequence. Friday's retail launch on October 23 will offer the first read on walk-in demand and whether Apple has restocked any in-store inventory beyond pre-orders. Apple's "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28 follows, which could shape the broader iPhone 18 narrative heading into earnings. Then on November 2, after the close, Apple reports Q4 FY2026 results; consensus sits at $1.99 EPS on $113.38 billion in revenue. That call is where analysts will press management on the Duo supply trajectory, holiday-quarter unit expectations, and whether the ASP thesis is tracking to the Bloomberg Intelligence estimates.

title: Dow outperforms as Wall Street rises, healthcare stocks lead gains
full_text:
By Sinéad Carew and Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Dow rose 1% on Tuesday, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500 while the healthcare sector provided Wall Street’s biggest boost and technology was its biggest drag.
Healthcare led gains among the S&P 500’s 11 major sector indexes, hitting a record high. Eli Lilly was the S&P 500’s biggest index point contributor while UnitedHealth, Merck & Co, Johnson & Johnson and Amgen helped boost the blue-chip Dow industrials.
Declines in megacap stocks pulled down the communication services sector. Energy shares underperformed as oil prices fell after touching a five-month high. Oil traders were weighing a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan’s army chief, a US-Iran mediator, against Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
TECH STOCKS TAKE A BREATHER
While the heavyweight technology sector eased 0.3%, it was the biggest index-point drag on the S&P 500 and kept the Nasdaq close to flat. Technology stocks had rebounded on Monday from a selloff last week when investors worried about steep spending and financing costs for AI developments.
"Equity investors are still a little skeptical around the AI trade and the ability for some of these companies to monetize their investments, so you’re seeing a bit of a rotation into other areas of the market," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, pointing to advances on Tuesday in small caps and healthcare companies.
"Investors are looking for other opportunities outside of tech, and healthcare is one of the beneficiaries of that," he said.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to 52,495.88, the S&P 500 gained 21.84 points, or 0.28%, to 7,712.57 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 6.07 points, or 0.02%, to 26,424.82.
The S&P 500 value index rose 0.9% compared with a 0.2% drop in its growth counterpart. The small-cap Russell 2000 index finished up 1.7%.
With a 1% gain, the financial services sector was the S&P 500’s second-biggest index point boost. Defensive sectors also outperformed, with real estate adding 1.7% and utilities climbing 1.2%.
A 1.7% drop in Netflix, a 1.6% decline in Meta and a 1% loss in Google parent Alphabet sent the communication services index down 0.9%.

Meta and Tesla are scheduled to report on Wednesday.
General Motors shares sank 6.8% after the automaker signaled pressure in coming months from higher commodity costs and lower truck sales.
3M rose 5.8% after the company said it was expanding its data-center partnership with Amazon and issued a warrant to an Amazon subsidiary to purchase 3M common stock worth over $521 million. The industrial conglomerate also raised its full-year profit forecast.
Credit reporting firm Equifax rallied 11.3% after it reported third-quarter profit above analysts’ estimates. Hasbro shares jumped 11.2% after the toymaker raised its full-year forecast for both overall revenue and its digital gaming business.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.04-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, where there were 114 new highs and 236 new lows.
On the Nasdaq, 3,245 stocks rose and 1,608 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 2.02-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 22 new 52-week highs and one new low, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 46 new highs and 266 new lows.

title: SpaceX and Tesla’s Terafab targets 2028 for volume chip production, Musk says
full_text:
Wall Street ends higher on surge in health care stocks, solid earnings
By Max A. Cherney
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The chip manufacturing joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla called Terafab aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Elon Musk said on a SpaceX conference call on Tuesday.
"I put big error bars on this because we don’t know if we will actually achieve this or not," Musk said, referring to the timeline.
The timeline is a rough schedule for a project that aims to produce 1 terawatt a year of computing power for AI and robotics, on a schedule Musk himself called "very aggressive." In the United States, cutting-edge logic factories can take three or more years to build.
Musk has described the planned complex in Texas as combining advanced manufacturing, packaging and testing of both advanced logic and memory chips in one facility.
On Tuesday, Musk said that internally, Terafab aims to have a first test chip, using static random-access memory (SRAM) circuits, functional in roughly May or June of next year at the Terafab research facility in Austin.
Chip manufacturers commonly fabricate SRAM circuits as a method of refining manufacturing process development.
MUSK CAUTIONS ON AMBITIOUS DATES
Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed. The SpaceX CEO described the Terafab timeline as the company’s aspiration and said the dates are "very aggressive."
"Let’s just say that outcome of achieving volume production is at least in the set of possible outcomes for Q3 or Q4 of ’28," Musk said. "So these are obviously like insanely fast time frames for chip production."
EQUIPMENT ACQUISITION CHALLENGE
On the SpaceX conference call, a sell-side analyst asked Musk whether SpaceX had placed orders for the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines produced only by the Dutch company ASML. The EUV machines are necessary to produce the most cutting-edge chips made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices.
Musk did not answer the question directly and said, "Now these were very aggressive dates, and we’re very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome."
One of the challenges Terafab faces is acquiring enough of the complex, expensive semiconductor manufacturing equipment from ASML or American suppliers such as Applied Materials and KLA.
Intel said in April that it would join the Terafab project to help accelerate Terafab’s goals. Intel also posted a photo of CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Musk shaking hands, saying it hosted the world’s richest man at its campus that month. The companies have not revealed how the collaboration would function in practice.
Earlier this month, Musk said there had been discussions about potential cooperation with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s largest advanced chip manufacturer. But Musk later said Terafab is committed to running the facility itself.

title: Amazon stockpiles Nvidia AI hardware ahead of power availability -Business Insider
full_text:

Investing.com -- Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) is fundamentally altering its hardware procurement playbook, agreeing to purchase billions of dollars in Nvidia Corp. graphics processors before its data centers are equipped with the power to run them. According to internal August emails obtained by Business Insider, the cloud giant established a new "Early Rack Receipt" program to take delivery of roughly $5 billion in Nvidia GB300 server racks at U.S. facilities ahead of final deployment, with expectations to accept an additional $3 billion in hardware each month for the foreseeable future.
The aggressive staging strategy highlights the extreme measures hyperscalers are taking to secure scarce artificial intelligence chips amid severe power grid constraints. Business Insider reported that finished equipment is currently being staged in intermediary warehouses because several Amazon Web Services sites lack the necessary utility capacity to energize the servers, leaving a portion of the hardware sitting idle as "dark GPUs."
This procurement shift carries substantial financial implications for the world’s largest cloud provider, which previously took ownership and recorded expenses for server racks only upon arrival at operational data centers. By taking delivery earlier in the supply chain, Amazon is tying up vast sums of capital in equipment before it can generate cloud rental revenue, placing immediate strain on corporate liquidity.
The capital-intensive strategy comes as Amazon’s broader AI infrastructure buildout pushes its financial resources to unprecedented levels. The company projects roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year, a figure that surpasses its Big Tech peers, contributing to a swing into negative free cash flow last quarter for the first time since 2023.
Despite the mounting cash flow pressures and tightening credit markets for data center financing, Amazon views early inventory absorption as a necessary trade-off to keep hardware out of competitors’ hands. An Amazon spokesperson defended the staging process as a routine "best business practice" designed to enable rapid installation once power capacity comes online, while disputing internal indications that the company lacked a clear path to bring the facilities live.
